Books Galore

By: Stenette Grosskopf | Commission

Proposal


Show: Carte Blanche

One Liner (Tonight on Carte Blanche...):
Books, books, books... Joburg's Literary District is brimming with books from across the world, from R15,000 first editions to religious pocket guides...

Unique Selling Point:
It’s 2024, the era of fast information, knowledge at our fingertips. An age when someone spots a headline on the internet and suddenly they’re an expert…
So how relevant are books? They’re a luxury for many in terms of money and time…
There is a belief that no-one is reading anymore, books are obsolete…
But you're wrong!


Summary:
Once in a while you downsize, you clear your bookshelves, drop some books at your local SPCA or bookshop…
But where do those end up?
This is not a story about waste or recycling… it’s a story about the overwhelming demand for books in the JHB CBD.

It’s called Johannesburg’s Literary District — with over 70 booksellers within an approximate 1km radius. These were mapped by Griffin Shea, a former AFP journalist who settled in South Africa. He opened Bridge Books in Helen Joseph street, Jhb and focusses mainly on local, African authors. He sources his books from many of the local dealers.

Present is a bookhunter, for the lack of a better word… he takes you into a building, down a passage into the dark basement. Opens a door to a room full of books, just some of his stash. He used to store them under Park Station, but the rats and fires caused serious damage.

The cheap books are sold on the street, mid-cost ones go to the more formal sellers and the very rare books are sold to exclusive book collectors, like James Findlay Collectables run from the basement of the Rand Club.



Further information:
The Joburg City Library is at the heart of the Literary District. But it has been closed since the Covid lockdown. It's deemed a fire hazard and big money is needed to revamp it. In the meantime, the hunger for books in the CBD is growing. With an influx of thousands of foreigners over the past decade, everything from school books to novels are in demand in the city.

In 1890 there were 11 booksellers in Joburg, including Juta & Co. CNA opened in 1895. Limbada & Company is the oldest bookshop still operational in the CBD. Today it is run by the grandson of the original owner.

The public library was established as early as 1889 and the current building was erected in 1935.

6639 – Books Galore!


City Waking up
VO
As Johannesburg starts bustling on a Friday morning, Present Njovo gets ready for a busy day.
UPS UNDER VISUALS
I always listen to what my customers are asking for. That’s what I go and look for.
VO
Present is a book hunter – traveling far and wide to find the perfect reads for his clients…
UPS




Present: Nice to meet you!

Masa: This is an impressive bookstore you’ve got here.

Present: Ja

Masa: Ooh I see you’ve got my favourite genre of books – political books.
VO
He sells everything from easy-read novels to memoirs and non-fiction… and even school textbooks.
UPS

PRESENT NJOVO


Masa: Where do you get all these books from?

Present: I do get them from different places. Some of the places I buy, some of the places I work, if they can’t pay me they pay me with books…

Masa: So they pay you with books, sometimes?

Present: Yes.
V/O
Present has been dealing in second-hand books for over a decade, and he doesn’t just sell them, he’s an avid reader himself.
UPS
Masa: Which are your favourite books?

Present: Ah my favourite books is this inspirational books. That can inspire my… that motivates me.
LINK
You may be surprised to learn that Present is not the only book trader in the CBD. In fact, books are big business here in the city. From informal vendors selling novels and textbooks to high end dealers selling collectables. Joburg is brimming with books.;


VO
The area around Park Station is known as the Literary District – within a mere three square kilometres you can find 71 different booksellers.

Griffin Shea is one of them.
UPS

GRIFFIN SHEA


Masa: Tell us a little bit about this space – Bridge Books.

Griffin: So, Bridge Books started eight years ago, around the corner from where we are now, mainly because I was having a huge problem finding African literature for myself and for my kids. And I sort of realised there had to be a different way to go about getting books into the hands of readers.
VO
As a former journalist it has never been about just selling books… He actively sought out other booksellers across the inner city and found them in all sorts of unlikely places.
UPS
Griffin: I think in Joburg, in general, we’re not great about putting signs. You know we don’t love to tell you where you are and the street signs don’t always help. So people just don’t know when you walk around that actually inside that spaza shop – yes I can get a quarter and some slap chips, but there’s also books. So, if you’re not in the neighbourhood every day and kinda knowing what’s here, you’d have no way to find out on your own.
VO
To draw visitors and help them navigate the area, Griffin put together a map of the district’s booksellers.
UPS
Griffin: That's why we're trying to put up the maps to let people know that, are you looking for Nigerian spirituals? There's a shop specializing in that right there. Do you need a Bible in Venda? There's a shop where you can buy a Bible in Venda around the corner too. Anything that you can imagine you can find within just a few blocks right here.
VO
And if it’s a one-of-a-kind publication you’re after… a good place to start is in the basement of the historic Rand Club.
UPS




James: I've been dealing for 27 years, and I focus on very valuable books, actually.

They’re historical and they're very limited. So first editions, sometimes the books are hundreds of years old as well, signed by very famous people and so on.
VO
James Findlay’s Collectable Books is a world away from the sidewalk sellers just around the corner.
UPS









JAMES FINDLAY


Masa: What's the most expensive book you have here?

James: Well, I've got this one in front of me, which is R150,000,

Masa: A R150,000?

James: Exactly.

Masa: I'm almost too scared to touch it.

James: And, it's just paper, you know, so it's quite interesting. You know, the objective value is that it's just paper, you can light a fire with it, but the intrinsic value is a story we tell ourselves.


VO
Published in 1738, this book describing indigenous Cape flora is a rare remnant of that era.
UPS
Masa: So what goes into the pricing is it the more rare it is, the older it is?

James: That’s a good question. So just because a book is old, doesn’t mean it’s valuable. It's a subjective pricing, so I decide what I think it is. It's not a science. Very much an art.
VO
With such a hefty pricetag, I daren’t even touch this book, but I can’t pass up the opportunity to hold a little – somewhat cheaper – bit of history.
UPS





Masa: May I touch one of these first edition Charles Dickens books?

James: Yes. With pleasure.

Masa: And the most expensive one. Thank you. James. (hehe)

James: There you go. And you see the binding is with 24 karat gold leaf. Oh, so that's real gold on the edges.


LINK
Masa: Way above my pay grade. So I'm going to give it back to you, James.

James: Thank you Masa.

Masa: At least I got to touch it.
VO
The Johannesburg City Library is at the heart of the district even though it has been closed to the public for over four years.
UPS


Griffin: It’s got a million & a half books inside…

Masa: a million and a half books

Griffin: And they don’t fit inside that building. So, actually underneath us, there’s three floors of books underneath the park.

Masa: Underneath the library?

Griffin: That we’re walking on top of the library right now as we go through the city.

Masa: So we’re walking on thousands of books right now.
VO
The library boasts – amongst others – an extensive sheet-music selection and a unique Africana collection.
UPS
Griffin: So there are books here that you cannot find anywhere else on the planet. So scholars and writers come from around the world to find the things that we keep in downtown Joburg.
VO
On the eastern edge of the Literary District is the city’s largest bookshop. – a booklovers’ paradise that is literally bursting at the seams.
UPS
Masa: Books and books and books. Good afternoon gentlemen.
VO
Geoffrey and Jonathan Klass have been selling books since the early 1970’s.
UPS
GEOFFREY KLASS


JONATHAN KLASS


Geoffrey: Books just became part of my life, I was collecting and going to book sales with my father when I was probably 7 or 8.

Jonathan: We grew up with collectibles and more books than a normal in a house. We had about 50 or 60,000 books or whatever we had.
VO
Today they have well over a million books, filling this building from corner to corner. No space for a mouse, let alone a film crew.
UPS



Masa: In terms of, like, being in the city, this is one place that we don't think of and think literature and books.

Jonathan: The thing is that we've always been in town. To us, this is home.

Geoffrey: The problem with the centre city is overcoming what I call the stigma of the Sandton curtain.

Masa: Haha tell me more!

Geoffrey: There has been an inbuilt perception in the public out there that the CBD has become a no go area. But the younger generation are overcoming that and they’re moving back into the centre city.
UPS
MUSIC
LINK
Running a business in Jo’burg CBD - it does come with its fair share of challenges. Just after our interview the lights went off, so cellphone light it is.

WOW - there’s so many treats here.
VO


While power cuts can get in the way of finding the perfect weekend read, vendors like Present face a whole different set of struggles.
UPS
Masa: Present, I hear that you used to store your books at Park Station, but then you stopped… Why?

Present: There’s no lights, there’s no drainage system inside. When it rains it’s sloppy. With books you have to be careful. It ended up, everything on fire because nobody is looking after this store room.
VO
Present has lost his entire book collection more than once over the past decade.
UPS
Present: It’s not far, just across the road.
VO
He now has books tucked away in various spots across the city.
UPS



Masa: You travel this route every day with a trolley?

Present: Yes everyday.

Masa: To the stall twice a day.

Present: Yeah.

Masa: You get your steps in hey?
VO
With the holidays fast approaching it’s peak season for the booksellers. A time of buying gifts… and also textbooks for the new school year.
UPS
Present: Here there are no rats. They don't come this side. They only, and they only play on the dustbins.

Masa: It's very dark.

Present: Yeah, that's the door.

Masa: Wow, Present. This is impressive.

Present: Yeah. That's my storage.

Masa: This is where you keep your babies.

Present: Yes, I used to sell on Plein and Wanderers, but just an hour.

Masa: But now this is your full time job you know.

Present: Yes. It's my full time job. There are other things that I'm crying that I also want to do. But you have to go stage by stage. But sometimes we want to run fast. We don't have patience. We are human beings.


Masa: Yeah. No, it will happen. It'll happen Present. I can feel it.
UPS
Grifin: If we keep telling ourselves the story that downtown Jo'burg is just crime and decay and collapsing buildings, then that is what it is, right? That is the story we're telling.
So if you have 60 bookshops in one kilometer, then actually you are Paris, right?

Masa: And they’re thriving bookshops, as well.

Griffin: Most of these bookstores are much more successful than me, like I have to hustle a side job to keep my life running. These guys are making money just selling books.





VO


UPS





VO
Promo 1
Can you imagine 71 booksellers in a 3 km area in the JHB CBD?

Griffin: Joburg, like in general, we're not great about putting signs, you know, like we don't love to tell you where you are necessarily.
So people just don't know when you walk around that actually inside that spaza shop. Yes. I can get a quarter and some slap tjips, but there's also books

We explore Egoli’s Literary District.

VO

UPS



VO
Promo 2

A walk of a different kind in Joburg’s CBD.

Masa: Oh my gosh, this is the book I used to read.
Present: Yeah, that's all right.
Masa: There was a whole series of these. You're really taking me down memory lane.
Present: (laughs)

Millions of Books tucked away in the unlikeliest of places.

VO


UPS




VO
Promo 3
From paperbacks at informal street vendors to highly collectable books.

Masa: R150,000?

James: Exactly. The objective value is that it's just paper. You can light a fire with it, but the intrinsic value is a story we tell ourselves.

Joburg’s Literary District is a booklovers paradise.

metadata.One Liner (Tonight on Carte Blanche...): Books, books, books... Joburg's Literary District is brimming with books from across the world, from R15,000 first editions to religious pocket guides...
metadata.Unique Selling Point: It’s 2024, the era of fast information, knowledge at our fingertips. An age when someone spots a headline on the internet and suddenly they’re an expert… So how relevant are books? They’re a luxury for many in terms of money and time… There is a belief that no-one is reading anymore, books are obsolete… But you're wrong!
metadata.Summary: Once in a while you downsize, you clear your bookshelves, drop some books at your local SPCA or bookshop… But where do those end up? This is not a story about waste or recycling… it’s a story about the overwhelming demand for books in the JHB CBD. It’s called Johannesburg’s Literary District — with over 70 booksellers within an approximate 1km radius. These were mapped by Griffin Shea, a former AFP journalist who settled in South Africa. He opened Bridge Books in Helen Joseph street, Jhb and focusses mainly on local, African authors. He sources his books from many of the local dealers. Present is a bookhunter, for the lack of a better word… he takes you into a building, down a passage into the dark basement. Opens a door to a room full of books, just some of his stash. He used to store them under Park Station, but the rats and fires caused serious damage. The cheap books are sold on the street, mid-cost ones go to the more formal sellers and the very rare books are sold to exclusive book collectors, like James Findlay Collectables run from the basement of the Rand Club.
metadata.Further information: The Joburg City Library is at the heart of the Literary District. But it has been closed since the Covid lockdown. It's deemed a fire hazard and big money is needed to revamp it. In the meantime, the hunger for books in the CBD is growing. With an influx of thousands of foreigners over the past decade, everything from school books to novels are in demand in the city. In 1890 there were 11 booksellers in Joburg, including Juta & Co. CNA opened in 1895. Limbada & Company is the oldest bookshop still operational in the CBD. Today it is run by the grandson of the original owner. The public library was established as early as 1889 and the current building was erected in 1935.
